match.reason: Neither bank point teaches identifying the writer's contention: eng-tone-mood covers tone and mood only, from a NSW Year 11 course, and eng-context-argument covers context and audience from Units 1 and 2 without naming the contention, so the new point is related to both rather than the same idea.

draft.title: Identifying the contention and tone
card: Contention
The main point the writer wants the audience to accept. It is the answer to the question: what is this writer arguing?
Audience
The people the writer is trying to persuade. Clues include where the piece appears and the words it uses to address readers.
Tone
The attitude the writer takes, such as urgent, sarcastic, calm or indignant. It is shown through word choices and the way sentences are shaped.
Context
The time, place and issue the piece responds to. Together with audience, it helps explain why the writer argues in this tone.
draft.remember: Before analysing methods, work out what is argued, to whom, in what tone and why now.

a.q: Which of these is a contention?
opts: Councils should ban cars from city centres
Cars are a common sight in many city centres
The writer describes traffic in a worried voice
The piece appears in a newspaper opinion section
a.why: A contention is the main point the writer wants accepted, and it says what should be believed or done. The tone option describes an attitude, not the point itself, and the other two give facts without arguing a position.
a.clue: Which one is a position the writer wants others to accept?

b.q: Priya, a Melbourne student, writes in a school newsletter to parents. She mocks the idea that homework builds character and says it should be cut back. Which pairing of tone and audience fits?
opts: Sarcastic tone, aimed at parents
Calm tone, aimed at government ministers
Sarcastic tone, aimed at the writer's own teachers
Calm tone, aimed at students in other states
b.why: Mocking an idea is a sarcastic tone, and a school newsletter to parents makes parents the audience. The calm options ignore the mockery, and the teachers option ignores where the piece appears.
b.clue: Mockery shows the tone. The newsletter shows who reads it.

a.best: Councils should ban cars from city centres

problems.detail: The stem says Priya writes 'to parents', so the audience half of the pairing is stated outright. Students only need to judge the tone, which weakens the audience test. Describing only the newsletter, without naming the readers, would make students infer the audience from where the piece appears.

b.q: Priya, a Melbourne student, writes a piece for the newsletter her school sends home each week. She mocks the idea that homework builds character and says it should be cut back. Which pairing of tone and audience fits?
opts: Sarcastic tone, aimed at families at her school
Calm tone, aimed at families at her school
Sarcastic tone, aimed at state politicians
Calm tone, aimed at state politicians
b.why: Mocking an idea is a sarcastic tone, and a newsletter sent home each week is read by the school's families, so they are the audience. The calm option with families gets the readers right but ignores the mockery, and the politicians options ignore where the piece appears.
